young.html: Samuel Beckett was an Irish writer who lived in Paris and wrote in both French and English. His most famous play is very strange and very simple.

In Waiting for Godot, two old friends, Vladimir and Estragon, wait beside a bare tree on a country road for someone called Godot. They don't really know who he is or why they're waiting. To pass the time they chat, argue, tell jokes, swap hats and play games. A boy comes to say Godot won't come today, but surely tomorrow. The next day they wait again. Godot never comes. The play is funny and sad at the same time, and people still argue about what it means.

young.html: The waiting game. Waiting can feel very long. Next time your family is waiting (in a car, in line, at the doctor's), invent a game to pass the time, as Vladimir and Estragon do. Afterward talk about it: what made the time go faster? Who or what were you really waiting for?

full.html: Samuel Beckett (1906–1989) was born near Dublin, studied French and Italian at Trinity College, and as a young man assisted James Joyce in Paris. During the Second World War he worked for the French Resistance and was honored for it afterward. He then began writing in French. En attendant Godot was published in 1952 and first staged in Paris in January 1953; Beckett's own English version followed in 1954. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969.
About quotations: the play was first published in the 1950s and is still under copyright, so this lesson describes it in our own words. See "Read the full text" above for where to find it.

Act I. On a country road with a single bare tree, Estragon struggles with his boot and Vladimir worries about the two thieves crucified beside Christ, since only one of the four Gospels says that one of them was saved. They are waiting for Godot. A pompous traveler, Pozzo, arrives driving his servant Lucky on a rope; ordered to "think," Lucky delivers a long, broken torrent of learned-sounding words. A boy brings word that Mr. Godot will not come this evening but surely tomorrow. Night falls. They agree to leave, and do not move.

Act II is the next evening. The tree has a few leaves. The friends wait again, though Estragon remembers little of the day before. Pozzo returns blind and Lucky has gone mute; Pozzo, asked when this happened, rejects the very question. The boy brings the same message and does not recognize them. Again they agree to go, and again they stay.

full.html: The play makes waiting itself the drama. Its pattern of near-repetition suggests a life in which people hope, pass the time and keep each other company while the meaning they wait for does not arrive, or has not yet.

Beckett refused to explain Godot. Some readers see God (the name suggests it, though Beckett denied a simple meaning), some see hope, death, or the human need for purpose. Critics grouped the play with the "Theatre of the Absurd," yet many audiences find it warm: two friends who stay together however bleak the road.
Calling it a play where nothing happens. Things do happen: quarrels, kindnesses, a cruelty, a reversal of fortune. What never happens is the one thing they wait for.

items: Pascal's Pensées, earlier on this ladder, described people filling time with diversions so as not to face their condition; Vladimir and Estragon are masters of diversion.
Chekhov, at the start of this era, wrote of people waiting and talking while their lives slip away.
Kafka, also in this era, told absurd situations in calm, plain words.

Augustine: Beckett was fond of a saying about the two thieves that is often credited to him (scholars have not found it in his writings): do not despair, one thief was saved; do not presume, one was lost.
What are you waiting for? How do you spend the waiting?
Why do Vladimir and Estragon stay together?
Is the play hopeful, despairing or both?
Why might a writer refuse to say what his play means?

questions: Who do you think Godot is? Why might Beckett never tell us?
Why do Vladimir and Estragon keep waiting, even when Godot never comes?
What is the best way to spend time while you wait for something?
The friends quarrel but always make up. What keeps a friendship going?
Pozzo changes completely between the acts. What does that suggest about life?
